description: We’re Team Pradyot. We’re interested in space and how we can use code and data to understand Earth better. We care about good design and testing whether our ideas hold up. We’re looking for teammates interested in development, research, UI/UX or storytelling. If you enjoy asking questions and figuring things out together, we’d like to work with you.
summary:
CINDERLINE is a web app that joins NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS fire hotspot records into one burning-activity calendar, from 2003 to 2025, for seven countries: the United States, Brazil, Australia, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Egypt.

The two instruments can’t be joined as they are. VIIRS has much smaller pixels and records many more hotspots. In one US week in September 2020, VIIRS recorded 96,345 detections and MODIS Aqua recorded 8,815. A raw combined record makes fire activity look as if it jumped when VIIRS took over. CINDERLINE converts VIIRS onto the MODIS Aqua scale. It learns the conversion from 2013–2017, picks a model on 2018–2019, and was tested once on 2020–2024. On those unseen US weeks, the gap to Aqua fell from +601% to +1.7%.

Users can look at a weekly or monthly calendar, draw their own area, compare seasons, and click any week to see the raw, converted and Aqua numbers behind it. We also found a weekly rhythm: US hotspot detections drop by about a third on Sundays in all three satellite records.

This matters now because MODIS is retiring. CINDERLINE keeps 20 years of fire history comparable with what comes after it.
details:
What it does

CINDERLINE answers a question that becomes harder as MODIS ends: was this fire season really unusual, or did the satellite change? It gives fire managers, researchers and students one calendar of burning activity from 2003 to 2025. MODIS Aqua observations cover 2003–2012, and VIIRS converted to the same scale covers 2013 onward. The site covers seven countries on very different fire regimes: the United States, Brazil, Australia, India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Egypt.

On the site, a user can:

  • read a week-by-year and month-by-year calendar and switch between the harmonized record and the raw, unconverted one to see the fake jump disappear
  • draw a rectangle or a point and radius to get a monthly calendar for their own area
  • click any week to open its evidence: what Terra, Aqua and VIIRS each detected, the converted value, the model used, and daily calibration intervals
  • compare a month or season against the same period in every other year
  • see historically high-activity periods translated into dates, and export them as a calendar file (.ics) for planning
  • browse flagged weeks that sit above or below their historical range
  • explore a 3D Earth view of annual activity, plus a 2024 layer of individual VIIRS observations
  • download CSVs and share links that reopen the same view

How the harmonization works

All hotspots come from the NASA FIRMS archive. Each record is cleaned, given a local date in the correct time zone, and placed on a 0.25° grid. We used MODIS Aqua as the reference because it crosses at about the same time of day as VIIRS on Suomi NPP. Results are therefore expressed as “Aqua-equivalent detections” rather than fires. A detection is a hot pixel, not a separate fire, and we say so everywhere.

We compared a naive join, a single ratio per country, and a stratified model. The stratified model uses separate ratios by country, day or night, and fire radiative power class. The data were split by time:

  • 2013–2017 to fit the conversion
  • 2018–2019 to choose a model for each country, after which the choice was locked
  • 2020–2024 as a test set, used once

Raw VIIRS was +357% to +3,136% over Aqua. We also applied the saved model, unchanged, to a second VIIRS satellite, NOAA-20. It stayed close to Aqua: US +1.3%, Nepal +0.6%, Bangladesh −0.5%.

Testing the conversion against its own weak points

We tried to break the method, and the site shows where it fails:

  • Egypt keeps a +51.7% bias because it has very few fires.
  • US agreement weakens over time, with weekly correlation falling from 0.97 in 2020 to 0.74 in 2024.
  • 2025 is past the test period and agrees less well.
  • A separate check showed that a model can get the yearly total right while getting the seasonal shape worse. In India the selected model cut the total-count error but bent the monthly pattern. The site reports both numbers, not just the flattering one.
  • Satellite outages appear as “no observation”, never as zero fire.

A finding the data revealed: the working week

We ran a separate test on each raw satellite record: do fewer hotspots appear on the local rest day? The pass rule was fixed before the full run.

  • In the United States, Sunday detections are 28% lower than the weekday average in Terra, 33% lower in Aqua and 22% lower in VIIRS.
  • The test passes in the US, Australia and Brazil. It does not pass in India, Nepal, Bangladesh or Egypt.
  • Fixed industrial heat sources in the US show no Sunday dip, which argues against a satellite scheduling effect.
  • The dip in total fire radiative power is smaller than the dip in detection counts, so on Sundays fewer fires are detected rather than every fire burning weaker.
  • An exploratory map found a strong pocket in northeast India, while the rest of India showed nothing.

This reproduces a pattern described in earlier research, now checked across three satellites and seven countries. It shows that people’s schedules leave a mark in the data. It does not prove who lit any particular fire.

Impact

MODIS on Terra and Aqua is near the end of its life. Trend studies, fire-season planning and land management depend on comparing this year with the past 20. CINDERLINE gives a tested, documented way to make that comparison across the change of instrument. It also shows clearly where the comparison is weaker, so users don’t put more trust in it than it deserves. A forest officer in Nepal can check whether this April was worse than usual. A researcher can download a consistent series. A student can see how satellites see fire.

Tools and technology

  • Data pipeline: Python with pandas, NumPy, PyArrow, timezonefinder and Matplotlib
  • Website: React and TypeScript built with Vite, three.js for the Earth view, served as static files on Cloudflare Pages, so there is no server and no login
  • Code, tests, methods and every report behind the numbers are in the public GitHub repository, with automated tests for both the pipeline and the web app

What makes it different

Most fire dashboards show raw counts. CINDERLINE is built around one question: is a change real, or did the instrument change? Every number links back to its evidence. The model was tested once on data it never saw, and its failures stay on the page next to its successes.
